summary:
This is the opening page of **Chapter 7, "A deep dive on Keras"** (PDF pp. 214–254). The "This chapter covers" box lists five topics:

- **The different ways to create Keras models**: the `Sequential` class, the **Functional API**, and **model subclassing** (section 7.2, from p.216).
- **The built-in Keras training and evaluation loops**, including **custom metrics and custom losses** (section 7.3, from p.230).
- **Keras callbacks** to further customize how training proceeds (p.232–p.234).
- **TensorBoard** for monitoring training and evaluation metrics over time (p.236).
- **Writing your own training and evaluation loops from scratch** (section 7.4, from p.238).

The introductory paragraph recaps what the reader already knows: the Sequential model, `Dense` layers, and the built-in APIs for training, evaluation and inference (`compile()`, `fit()`, `evaluate()`, `predict()`). In chapter 3 the reader also learned to inherit from the `Layer` class to create custom layers. The sentence continues on p.215, which mentions using the gradient APIs of TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch for a step-by-step training loop, and explains that later applications need much more than `Sequential` and the default `fit()`.

**How to use this page:** treat the bullet list as a roadmap. The chapter follows Keras's principle of *progressive disclosure of complexity* (p.215): each section adds flexibility on top of the previous one. You will get the most from it if you are comfortable with `fit()` and custom `Layer` subclasses.

concepts.name: Sequential model
concepts.definition: A Keras model built as a linear stack of layers.
concepts.technical: Covered in section 7.2.1 (p.216) as the simplest of three model-building APIs.
concepts.significance: The starting point the reader already knows.
concepts.misconception: That it can express any architecture. Multi-input/output or branching models need the Functional API.

concepts.name: Functional API
concepts.definition: Building Keras models by calling layers on symbolic inputs to form a graph.
concepts.intuition: Wiring components together like a circuit diagram.
concepts.significance: Handles multi-input, multi-output and non-linear topologies.
concepts.example: inputs = keras.Input(...); x = layers.Dense(64)(inputs); model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
concepts.misconception: That it is a different framework. It produces the same keras.Model objects.

concepts.name: Model subclassing
concepts.definition: Defining a model by subclassing keras.Model and writing its call() method.
concepts.intuition: Writing the forward pass by hand for maximum freedom.
concepts.significance: The most flexible option, at the cost of some built-in conveniences.
concepts.misconception: That subclassing is always better. Chapter 7 stresses using the right tool for the job (p.229).

takeaways: Chapter 7 covers three ways to build Keras models: Sequential, Functional API, and model subclassing.
It shows how to customize built-in loops with custom metrics, losses and callbacks, and how to monitor them with TensorBoard.
It ends with writing training and evaluation loops from scratch.
It builds on compile()/fit()/evaluate()/predict() and the custom Layer subclassing from chapter 3.
